current_answer: Jev is a hosted TypeSafe System One model for bounded Choice, Score, or Noul decisions; code owns thresholds, permissions, actions, and fallback. The 24 September builder-fit branch remains conditional: pilot only after task, access, data, and fallback checks; wait on unknown terms or account facts; stop for unsafe or irreversible automation. A 25 September support-ticket recipe shows how to test Choice on a builder’s own labelled cases, including out-of-scope, ambiguous, sensitive, and high-confidence wrong-route cases, with errors reported alongside review load. It is a protocol only: no Jev call, result, threshold, or production suitability was measured.

catalogue_card.question: What can I build with Jev, what alternatives exist, and where can I use it at what cost?
catalogue_card.text: Start with a bounded decision and the pilot/wait/stop gate. Before automatic routing, use the 25 September support-ticket protocol to test labelled cases, including out-of-scope and high-confidence errors, and record review load. This pool has no measured Jev result. Earlier alternatives and product audits remain bounded and unchanged.

summary: Choice, Score, and Noul cover routing, scoring, and yes/no gates inside ordinary code.

The current official record names Jev 1.13 (jev-1.13.0), with jev-latest and jev-preview currently pointing to it, a POST https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone endpoint, $0.042 per million input tokens and free output.

TypeSafe lists 250,000 tokens/second, 1,200 requests/minute, a 64k request context, a 32k state-plus-longest-question limit, and text-only input; access eligibility and some provider terms remain account checks.
The 24 September builder branch is pilot, route fallback, substitute, wait, or stop. It is a decision guide, not an access, adoption, or performance measurement.
The 22 September alternatives audit keeps model identity, interface compatibility, runtime/privacy, workflow role, and trade-offs separate.

The adapter is the closest interface substitute but calls other LLM providers; SemIf is an independent local experiment; jevlike is a trainable scorer; GLiClass is a classifier; a structured-output LLM is a schema/generation baseline.
No verified open-weight Jev model was found in the six direct checks on 22 September 2026. This is a verification-status finding, not proof that no such model exists.

The 23 September bounded adoption audit found no verified production product in the checked sources. killmyidea has direct Jev wiring and public-deployment metadata, but access and adoption remain unverified.

Jev Showcase is an unofficial local/Docker integration, the TypeSafe playground tool router is an explicitly mocked official-repository demo, jev-usecases is an MIT reference harness with an explicit non-production disclaimer, and Awesome Jev is a lead index only.
Proposed maintenance cadences are not measured analytics or automated monitoring. Historical values should be marked unknown when their current source is stale or unreachable.

The 25 September Choice workload-evaluation protocol defines separate consecutive and challenge cohorts, adjudicated gold labels, pinned test inputs and model, fair local baselines, review fallback, and failure-inclusive denominators; all result cells remain blank.
uncertainty: A Join Waitlist link was observed on 20 Sep but not in the fetched home text on 24 Sep; this does not prove open signup. Console login eligibility, credit grant, and API-key access remain unverified.
OpenRouter quotas/fees/data controls, Cloudflare dashboard pricing/retention, Vercel availability, and independent proxy terms/retention remain incomplete.

TypeSafe legal pages distinguish no training/fine-tuning on Input without consent from service, billing, telemetry, fraud/abuse, legal processing, and ordinary retention; no Jev-specific retention duration is published here.
Speed, calibration, availability, gateway uptime panels, and provider claims are workload- or route-dependent. No checked public source established a commercial production deployment or customer use.

The alternatives audit has direct evidence for the adapter, SemIf, jevlike, GLiClass, and the structured-output baseline, but current model parity, full primitive compatibility, privacy/data path, exact licence where not stated, cost, latency, and maintenance remain unknown where the sources are silent.
The mini-jev repository was not successfully checked in the alternatives refresh; do not carry its historical label forward as a current fact.
The killmyidea repository shows a Jev endpoint/model path and deployment metadata, but the public host was not accessible to the checker; current operation and adoption remain unknown.

No checked direct source names a paying customer, operator, case study, production trace, package release in use, or independent usage measure for the audited leads. No authenticated Jev call was made.
No independent workload measurement, common comparison, or authenticated Jev call was run in these records. Live performance, accuracy, calibration, and fallback success remain unknown.
The maintenance rules are proposed page-owner rules. They do not establish source freshness, analytics, account access, gateway quotas, customer usage, or automated change detection.
The 23 Sep TypeSafe MCA revision date is visible, but the exact Sep 19-to-23 clause diff is unknown; review the current MCA, DPA, and selected route before sensitive data.

The independent proxy self-reports $0.42/M input for $5/$10/$20 packs, $0.35/M for $50, and $0.25/M for $100 on 24 Sep; whether these tiers already existed on 20 Sep, and actual purchase and retention terms, are unknown.

The support-ticket protocol has not been executed. Workload-specific false-route, out-of-scope, high-impact, latency, review-load, token-cost, and human-resolution outcomes remain unknown. No confidence cutoff is validated for deployment.
